units.title: Trope 1: What trope is
units.subtitle: Cantillation marks: what they are, why there are many melodies, rulers and connectors

steps.label: Trope
steps.text: Look closely at a printed Torah verse. Besides the vowels, small marks sit above and below the words. These are the te'amim, the accents. In English and Yiddish they are usually called trope.
steps.src: Genesis 1:1. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Names: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

verse.he_t: בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים אֵ֥ת הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם וְאֵ֥ת הָאָֽרֶץ׃
verse.he: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ

steps.text: The same verse with the trope taken out. The letters and vowels are exactly the same. The trope adds a layer on top.
steps.src: Genesis 1:1. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA)

verse.he_t: בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים אֵ֥ת הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם וְאֵ֥ת הָאָֽרֶץ׃
verse.he: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ

steps.text: The marks do three jobs. They show which syllable is stressed. They group words into phrases, like commas and periods. And each mark stands for a short tune.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: The Talmud finds the te'amim already in Ezra's public Torah reading. It reads the words "and caused them to understand the reading" (Nehemiah 8:8) as the cantillation that makes the verses clear.
steps.src: Talmud Nedarim 37b (William Davidson translation on Sefaria)

steps.text: The written marks came later. Scholars called the Masoretes, working mostly in Tiberias, added vowels and te'amim to the text between about the 7th and 10th centuries CE. The Aleppo Codex, about 930 CE, is the best-known example.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑ (scholarly dating)

steps.text: Chanting is part of learning, not decoration. The Talmud criticizes reading Torah without a melody. One reason it gives: the tune helps you remember what you learned.
steps.src: Talmud Megillah 32a (William Davidson translation on Sefaria)

steps.text: A mark is not a single note. It names a short tune, and the tune depends on the book and the community. This app teaches each mark's name, shape and job. Melodies come only from real recordings, like your cantor's.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

lessons.title: One set of marks, many melodies
lessons.subtitle: Torah, Haftarah, scrolls

steps.label: Melodies
steps.text: The same marks are sung to different melodies, depending on what is read. Ashkenazi tradition has separate melodies for the Torah, the Haftarah, Esther, Lamentations, and the other three scrolls (Ruth, Song of Songs, Ecclesiastes). The Torah also has a special melody for the High Holy Days.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: The Haftarah is the reading from the Prophets after the Torah reading on Shabbat and festivals. Same marks as the Torah, a different tune. Its blessings are in this app's Torah service unit.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: Esther is chanted on Purim and Lamentations (Eicha) on Tisha B'Av, each with its own melody.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: Communities differ too. Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Yemenite and other communities sing different tunes, and some marks have different names. This app uses the Ashkenazi names.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: Three books, Psalms, Proverbs and Job, use a different set of marks. This course covers the system used in the other 21 books of the Tanakh.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: So you learn each mark once: its name, its shape and its job. Its tune is a second layer, learned once per melody from a recording.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.label: Two kinds
steps.text: Trope marks come in two kinds. Disjunctive marks (mafsikim) mark a pause; they are often called kings or rulers. Conjunctive marks (m'shartim, "servants") join a word to the next one.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: Every verse ends with sof pasuk, "end of verse": a short line called silluk under the stressed syllable of the last word, then two dots after it.
steps.src: Genesis 1:1. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA)

verse.he_t: בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים אֵ֥ת הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם וְאֵ֥ת הָאָֽרֶץ׃
verse.he: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ

steps.text: Most verses split into two halves at etnachta, the strongest pause inside a verse. Here the first half is the first three words. Of the 58 Genesis verses in this app, 57 have an etnachta.
steps.src: Genesis 1:1. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Count: this app's verses (Genesis 2:1 has none)

verse.he_t: בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים אֵ֥ת הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם וְאֵ֥ת הָאָֽרֶץ׃
verse.he: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ

steps.text: Each half is divided again by smaller rulers, and connectors lead into them. A verse works like a sentence with commas inside its two halves.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

verse.he_t: וַיִּבְרָ֨א אֱלֹהִ֤ים ׀ אֶת־הָֽאָדָם֙ בְּצַלְמ֔וֹ בְּצֶ֥לֶם אֱלֹהִ֖ים בָּרָ֣א אֹת֑וֹ זָכָ֥ר וּנְקֵבָ֖ה בָּרָ֥א אֹתָֽם׃
verse.he: וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים בָּרָא אֹתוֹ זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בָּרָא אֹתָם

steps.text: Tipcha is a ruler that usually comes just before etnachta or sof pasuk. Mercha is a connector that often leads into tipcha. In this verse's second half: mercha, tipcha, mercha, then sof pasuk.
steps.src: Genesis 1:1. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

verse.he_t: בְּרֵאשִׁ֖ית בָּרָ֣א אֱלֹהִ֑ים אֵ֥ת הַשָּׁמַ֖יִם וְאֵ֥ת הָאָֽרֶץ׃
verse.he: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ

units.title: Trope 2: The marks
units.subtitle: One lesson per family: shape, ruler or connector, and the marks it pairs with

steps.label: Zakef katon
steps.text: Zakef katon is a ruler written above the word: two dots, one over the other. Its pause is smaller than etnachta's. Each half of a verse is often split again at a zakef katon.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: Munach is a connector written below the word, shaped like a corner. It often leads into zakef katon: in this app's verses that pair comes 39 times.
steps.src: Genesis 1:2. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

verse.he_t: וְהָאָ֗רֶץ הָיְתָ֥ה תֹ֙הוּ֙ וָבֹ֔הוּ וְחֹ֖שֶׁךְ עַל־פְּנֵ֣י תְה֑וֹם וְר֣וּחַ אֱלֹהִ֔ים מְרַחֶ֖פֶת עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הַמָּֽיִם׃
verse.he: וְהָאָרֶץ הָיְתָה תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ וְחֹשֶׁךְ עַל־פְּנֵי תְהוֹם וְרוּחַ אֱלֹהִים מְרַחֶפֶת עַל־פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם

steps.text: Among the rulers inside a verse, only tipcha is more common here than zakef katon (114 and 64 times).
steps.src: Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

steps.label: Zakef gadol
steps.text: Zakef gadol is a ruler above the word: the two dots of zakef katon with a short vertical line beside them. It stands in for zakef katon when no connector comes before it.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: It is rare: 4 times in this app's verses. In every one, the word before it has no connector.
steps.src: Genesis 2:9. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

verse.he_t: וַיַּצְמַ֞ח יְהֹוָ֤ה אֱלֹהִים֙ מִן־הָ֣אֲדָמָ֔ה כׇּל־עֵ֛ץ נֶחְמָ֥ד לְמַרְאֶ֖ה וְט֣וֹב לְמַאֲכָ֑ל וְעֵ֤ץ הַֽחַיִּים֙ בְּת֣וֹךְ הַגָּ֔ן וְעֵ֕ץ הַדַּ֖עַת ט֥וֹב וָרָֽע׃
verse.he: וַיַּצְמַח יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהִים מִן־הָאֲדָמָה כׇּל־עֵץ נֶחְמָד לְמַרְאֶה וְטוֹב לְמַאֲכָל וְעֵץ הַחַיִּים בְּתוֹךְ הַגָּן וְעֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע

steps.label: Revia
steps.text: Revia is a ruler written above the word as a single diamond-shaped dot. Its pause is smaller than zakef katon's.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: Munach leads into revia too (10 times in this app's verses). The same connector can serve different rulers.
steps.src: Genesis 1:26. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

verse.he_t: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֔ים נַֽעֲשֶׂ֥ה אָדָ֛ם בְּצַלְמֵ֖נוּ כִּדְמוּתֵ֑נוּ וְיִרְדּוּ֩ בִדְגַ֨ת הַיָּ֜ם וּבְע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֗יִם וּבַבְּהֵמָה֙ וּבְכׇל־הָאָ֔רֶץ וּבְכׇל־הָרֶ֖מֶשׂ הָֽרֹמֵ֥שׂ עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃
verse.he: וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ וְיִרְדּוּ בִדְגַת הַיָּם וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וּבַבְּהֵמָה וּבְכׇל־הָאָרֶץ וּבְכׇל־הָרֶמֶשׂ הָרֹמֵשׂ עַל־הָאָרֶץ

steps.label: Pashta
steps.text: Pashta is a ruler written above the last letter of the word, slanting to the left. It often comes right before zakef katon.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑. 22 times in this app's verses

steps.text: When the stress is not on the last syllable, pashta is written twice: once over the stressed syllable and once on the last letter. That happens 9 times in this app's verses.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑. Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

steps.text: Mahpach is a connector written below the word, shaped like a sideways V. It often leads into pashta (22 times here).
steps.src: Genesis 1:31. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

verse.he_t: וַיַּ֤רְא אֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת־כׇּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֔ה וְהִנֵּה־ט֖וֹב מְאֹ֑ד וַֽיְהִי־עֶ֥רֶב וַֽיְהִי־בֹ֖קֶר י֥וֹם הַשִּׁשִּֽׁי׃ {פ}
verse.he: וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־כׇּל־אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה וְהִנֵּה־טוֹב מְאֹד וַיְהִי־עֶרֶב וַיְהִי־בֹקֶר יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי {פ}

steps.label: Yetiv
steps.text: Yetiv is a ruler written below the word, before its first letter. It takes pashta's place on some short words with no connector before them.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: Yetiv looks a lot like mahpach. The difference is where it sits: yetiv comes before the first letter. It appears 9 times in this app's verses.
steps.src: Genesis 2:23. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

verse.he_t: וַיֹּ֘אמֶר֮ הָֽאָדָם֒ זֹ֣את הַפַּ֗עַם עֶ֚צֶם מֵֽעֲצָמַ֔י וּבָשָׂ֖ר מִבְּשָׂרִ֑י לְזֹאת֙ יִקָּרֵ֣א אִשָּׁ֔ה כִּ֥י מֵאִ֖ישׁ לֻֽקְחָה־זֹּֽאת׃
verse.he: וַיֹּאמֶר הָאָדָם זֹאת הַפַּעַם עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי לְזֹאת יִקָּרֵא אִשָּׁה כִּי מֵאִישׁ לֻקְחָה־זֹּאת

steps.label: Tevir
steps.text: Tevir is a ruler written below the word. It often comes before tipcha (11 times in this app's verses).
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑. Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

steps.text: Darga is a connector below the word, shaped like a zigzag. It often leads into tevir (7 times here). Mercha can lead into tevir too (10 times).
steps.src: Genesis 2:8. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

verse.he_t: וַיִּטַּ֞ע יְהֹוָ֧ה אֱלֹהִ֛ים גַּן־בְּעֵ֖דֶן מִקֶּ֑דֶם וַיָּ֣שֶׂם שָׁ֔ם אֶת־הָֽאָדָ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָצָֽר׃
verse.he: וַיִּטַּע יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהִים גַּן־בְּעֵדֶן מִקֶּדֶם וַיָּשֶׂם שָׁם אֶת־הָאָדָם אֲשֶׁר יָצָר

steps.label: Geresh
steps.text: Geresh is a ruler written above the word, one slanted stroke. Gershayim is the same with two strokes. Both mark small pauses, and geresh often comes before revia.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑. 6 geresh-revia pairs in this app's verses

steps.text: Kadma is a connector with the same shape as pashta, but it sits over the stressed syllable, not the last letter. Kadma before geresh is a pair called kadma v'azla.
steps.src: Genesis 1:26. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

verse.he_t: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֔ים נַֽעֲשֶׂ֥ה אָדָ֛ם בְּצַלְמֵ֖נוּ כִּדְמוּתֵ֑נוּ וְיִרְדּוּ֩ בִדְגַ֨ת הַיָּ֜ם וּבְע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֗יִם וּבַבְּהֵמָה֙ וּבְכׇל־הָאָ֔רֶץ וּבְכׇל־הָרֶ֖מֶשׂ הָֽרֹמֵ֥שׂ עַל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃
verse.he: וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ וְיִרְדּוּ בִדְגַת הַיָּם וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וּבַבְּהֵמָה וּבְכׇל־הָאָרֶץ וּבְכׇל־הָרֶמֶשׂ הָרֹמֵשׂ עַל־הָאָרֶץ

steps.label: Rarer marks
steps.text: These marks appear less often than the ones so far (together 20 times in this app's verses). Learn their shapes now; the tunes come later.
steps.src: Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

steps.text: Segol is a ruler of three dots above the last letter. Zarka, a zigzag above the last letter, often comes before it, as here.
steps.src: Genesis 2:23. Hebrew: Miqra according to the Masorah (Sefaria, CC-BY-SA). Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

verse.he_t: וַיֹּ֘אמֶר֮ הָֽאָדָם֒ זֹ֣את הַפַּ֗עַם עֶ֚צֶם מֵֽעֲצָמַ֔י וּבָשָׂ֖ר מִבְּשָׂרִ֑י לְזֹאת֙ יִקָּרֵ֣א אִשָּׁ֔ה כִּ֥י מֵאִ֖ישׁ לֻֽקְחָה־זֹּֽאת׃
verse.he: וַיֹּאמֶר הָאָדָם זֹאת הַפַּעַם עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי לְזֹאת יִקָּרֵא אִשָּׁה כִּי מֵאִישׁ לֻקְחָה־זֹּאת

steps.text: Telisha gedola is a ruler above the first letter of the word. Telisha ketana has a similar shape but is a connector, above the last letter. Pazer is a ruler above the word.
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

steps.text: Shalshelet, a zigzag above the word, is the rarest: it appears only four times in the Torah (Genesis 19:16, 24:12, 39:8 and Leviticus 8:23).
steps.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tm-sof_pasuk.name: Sof pasuk (silluk)
tm-sof_pasuk.pos: below the stressed syllable of the last word, then two dots after the word
tm-sof_pasuk.note: Ends every verse. Silluk looks like the meteg, a small vertical line; the two dots after the word make it certain.
tm-sof_pasuk.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑ page to check; Unicode encoding as in Sefaria's Masorah text

tm-etnachta.name: Etnachta
tm-etnachta.note: The main pause inside a verse: it splits most verses in two.
tm-etnachta.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑ page to check; Unicode encoding as in Sefaria's Masorah text

tm-tipcha.name: Tipcha
tm-tipcha.note: Usually comes just before etnachta or sof pasuk.
tm-tipcha.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑ page to check; Unicode encoding as in Sefaria's Masorah text

tm-mercha.name: Mercha
tm-mercha.note: Often leads into tipcha, or into silluk at the end of a verse.
tm-mercha.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑ page to check; Unicode encoding as in Sefaria's Masorah text

tm-munach.name: Munach
tm-munach.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑ page to check; Unicode encoding as in Sefaria's Masorah text

opts: The vowel dots under the letters
Marks that show stress, phrasing and a short tune
The scribe's crowns on the scroll letters
tq-t1-what.why: Vowels are a separate system. Trope marks sit alongside them and do three jobs.
tq-t1-what.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t1-neh.q: Which verse does the Talmud read as including the te'amim?
tq-t1-neh.why: Nehemiah 8:8 describes Ezra's reading; Nedarim 37b takes "caused them to understand" as the cantillation.

tq-t1-meg.q: In Megillah 32a, what is one benefit of chanting?
opts: It helps you remember what you learned
tq-t1-meg.why: The Gemara explains that the tune helps the learner remember.

tq-t2-haf.q: Is the Haftarah chanted to the Torah melody?
tq-t2-haf.why: The Prophets use the same marks as the Torah, sung to the Haftarah melody.
tq-t2-haf.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-purim.q: Which book has its own melody for Purim?
tq-t2-purim.why: Esther is read on Purim with its own melody.
tq-t2-purim.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-comm.q: What differs between Ashkenazi and Sephardi reading?
opts: The tunes, and some mark names
The Hebrew words of the Torah
tq-t2-comm.why: The text is shared. The tunes and some names of the marks differ.
tq-t2-comm.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

opts: Splits the verse into two halves
Joins a word to the next
tq-t3-et.why: Etnachta is the main pause inside the verse.
tq-t3-et.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t3-mer.q: Is mercha a ruler or a connector?
opts: A ruler: it marks a pause
A connector: it leads into the next word
tq-t3-mer.why: Mercha is a conjunctive mark, often leading into tipcha.
tq-t3-mer.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-1a.why: Zakef katon's two dots sit above the word.
tq-t2-1a.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-1b.q: Which connector often leads into zakef katon?
tq-t2-1b.why: Munach. Tipcha and etnachta are rulers, not connectors.
tq-t2-1b.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-2a.q: When does zakef gadol appear instead of zakef katon?
opts: When no connector comes before it
At the end of a verse
tq-t2-2a.why: Zakef gadol is the form of zakef used without a connector before it.
tq-t2-2a.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-3a.why: Two dots above is zakef katon; the corner below is munach.
tq-t2-3a.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

opts: On the last letter of the word
tq-t2-4a.why: Pashta goes on the last letter, and on the stressed syllable too when that isn't last.
tq-t2-4a.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-4b.q: Mahpach or munach: which is shaped like a sideways V?
tq-t2-4b.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-5a.q: Yetiv and mahpach look alike. How do you tell them apart?
opts: Yetiv sits before the first letter
Yetiv is always the last word
tq-t2-5a.why: Yetiv is placed before the word's first letter.
tq-t2-5a.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-6a.q: Which ruler does tevir often come before?
tq-t2-6a.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑. Count: this app's 58 Genesis verses (Masorah text on Sefaria)

tq-t2-6b.q: Is darga a ruler or a connector?
tq-t2-6b.why: Darga is a connector; it leads into tevir.
tq-t2-6b.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-7a.q: Kadma and pashta look the same. What tells them apart?
opts: Where they sit: pashta on the last letter, kadma on the stressed syllable
tq-t2-7a.why: Same shape, different position. Two strokes is gershayim.
tq-t2-7a.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-7b.q: What is the pair kadma v'azla?
tq-t2-7b.why: In this pair the geresh is called azla.
tq-t2-7b.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-8a.q: How many times does shalshelet appear in the Torah?
tq-t2-8a.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑

tq-t2-8b.q: Telisha gedola and telisha ketana: which is the connector?
tq-t2-8b.why: Ketana (small) connects; gedola (big) is a ruler.
tq-t2-8b.src: Joshua R. Jacobson, Chanting the Hebrew Bible (JPS, 2002) ⚑
